title: Habakkuk 1:12–17
context: Habakkuk answers the LORD with a second complaint. He begins by confessing who God is, everlasting, “my Holy One,” the Rock, and he accepts that the LORD has appointed the Chaldeans “for judgment” (1:12). Yet he presses a harder question: how can a God whose eyes are too pure to look on evil stay silent while the treacherous swallow those more righteous than they (1:13)? He pictures the conqueror as a fisherman who hauls in nations with hook, net, and dragnet, then sacrifices to his net because it makes him rich (1:14–16), and he asks whether this will go on forever (1:17). Shared ground: both traditions read the complaint as faith appealing to God’s character, and both hear the fishing imagery as a portrait of conquest and the idolatry of power.

verses.text: Aren’t you from everlasting, LORD my God, my Holy One? We will not die. LORD, you have appointed them for judgment. You, Rock, have established him to punish.
verses.arminianNotes: “Aren’t you from everlasting, LORD my God, my Holy One? We will not die.” Habakkuk anchors his second complaint in who God is. Arminian readers see trust grasping the covenant relationship and drawing hope that the judgment is meant to correct rather than destroy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the confession “you have appointed them for judgment”: Habakkuk acknowledges God’s ordaining of Babylon’s role even as he struggles with it. Shared ground: both traditions read “We will not die” as faith in the LORD’s covenant faithfulness, hear “Rock” as a title of steadfast protection, and see the coming judgment as purposeful.

verses.text: You who have purer eyes than to see evil, and who cannot look on perversity, why do you tolerate those who deal treacherously and keep silent when the wicked swallows up the man who is more righteous than he,
verses.arminianNotes: “You who have purer eyes than to see evil, and who cannot look on perversity, why do you tolerate those who deal treacherously?” Arminian readers see the prophet pressing a real moral question: a holy God appears to permit greater wickedness to swallow lesser, and faith is allowed to ask why.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same tension and hold that God’s purity is not compromised by his governing use of the wicked, though his reasons may remain hidden for a time. Shared ground: both traditions read “purer eyes than to see evil” as meaning that God cannot approve evil, not that he is unaware of it, and both value the prophet’s honesty.

verses.text: and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things that have no ruler over them?
verses.arminianNotes: “and make men like the fish of the sea, like the creeping things that have no ruler over them?” Arminian readers hear Habakkuk lamenting the way people are treated as prey when protection fails, and they see in the complaint a concern for human dignity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Habakkuk attributes even this to God (“make men”), voicing honest perplexity at God’s providence rather than denying it. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as continuing the question of verse 13, and both see the image of creatures with no ruler as a lament over the vulnerability of the nations before Babylon.

verses.text: He takes up all of them with the hook. He catches them in his net and gathers them in his dragnet. Therefore he rejoices and is glad.
verses.arminianNotes: “He takes up all of them with the hook.” The Chaldean conqueror is pictured as a fisherman hauling in nations. Arminian readers see a ruthless power delighting in its own success, “Therefore he rejoices and is glad,” with no sense of answerability to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the conqueror’s joy as the pride God will humble, and note that the one who seems to control the net is himself under God’s hand. Shared ground: both traditions read the fishing imagery as a picture of conquest and deportation, and both see the conqueror’s gladness as heartless triumph over human suffering.

verses.text: Therefore he sacrifices to his net and burns incense to his dragnet, because by them his life is luxurious and his food is good.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore he sacrifices to his net and burns incense to his dragnet.” Arminian readers see the logical end of making strength one’s god (1:11): the conqueror worships the means of his success, giving his gratitude to tools rather than to God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see idolatry in its essence: the creature trusts and worships what serves its luxury rather than the Creator who gives all things. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a portrait of the idolatry of power and prosperity, and both note that whether actual rites to weapons lie behind it is uncertain; the point is clear either way.

verses.text: Will he therefore continually empty his net, and kill the nations without mercy?
verses.arminianNotes: “Will he therefore continually empty his net, and kill the nations without mercy?” Arminian readers hear an appeal to God’s justice: surely the one who uses Babylon will not let it go on slaughtering forever.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the question as preparing for the LORD’s answer in chapter 2: God’s purpose has a limit and a time, and Babylon’s cruelty will be judged. Shared ground: both traditions read the complaint as faith appealing to God’s character, and both see the question of killing “without mercy” as answered by the vision and the woes that follow.
